acta_materia_M1_M2_M3_s3v5 backbone item

The [0001] orientation fractures in compression at ~355 MPa without yielding, and flows in tension at ~72 MPa (serrated ~52-80) to ~45% plastic strain. The two numbers are a fracture stress and a flow stress, not two yield stresses, so they are not a yield ratio; what they show is that the orientation has a deformation route available in tension that is absent in compression, and the kink bands in F10b are what identifies it.

what this trace ends up asserting

The [0001] orientation fractures in compression at ~355 MPa without yielding, and flows in tension at ~72 MPa (serrated ~52-80) to ~45% plastic strain. The two numbers are a fracture stress and a flow stress, not two yield stresses, so they are not a yield ratio; what they show is that the orientation has a deformation route available in tension that is absent in compression, and the kink bands in F10b are what identifies it.

limits still attached at the end:

  • A fracture stress and a flow stress are different quantities; dividing them gives a number with no mechanical meaning.
  • Whether kinking is also available in compression and merely pre-empted by fracture is not established here.
  • The 355 MPa (RT) / 255 MPa (300C) values are compressive fracture stresses (no yielding occurs in compression for [0001]), while the ~72 MPa value is a tensile flow-stress onset (serrated 52-80 MPa) with fracture only after ~45% plastic strain; no tensile fracture stress or compressive flow/yield stress for [0001] is reported, so no same-kind pair exists in the observations to substitute. The two numbers therefore cannot be combined into a single ratio or yield comparison -- the valid conclusion is qualitative: [0001] has a ductile deformation route in tension (kink-banded, non-basal) that is absent in compression, not a quantitative measure of how much 'weaker' one mode is than the other.

No limit was dropped at any seam in this trace.

acta_materia_com_o23_o24
step 1 · MECH:tensile
Tensile [0001] test at RT: the flow stress starts at ~72 MPa, is serrated between ~52 and ~80 MPa, and the specimen reaches ~45% plastic strain before fracture
step 2 · OM
The tensile gauge is filled with fine bands inclined to the [0001] tensile direction, across which the marked basal-plane trace kinks
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about PRF/service_capability, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane otherdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength conditional mechanism
key — the combining proposition
Placing the tensile curve and the optical micrograph side by side ties the mechanical response of the [0001] tension test (serrated flow stress ~52-80 MPa, ~45% plastic strain to fracture) to a specific microstructural mechanism: the same gauge section that produced that large-strain serrated response is filled with fine bands inclined to the tensile axis across which the marked basal-plane trace kinks. Together this supports that the large tensile ductility recorded mechanically is accommodated by kink-band formation in the gauge, rather than by some other unseen deformation mode.
limits
  • The OM image is a single post-test (or single-state) view of the gauge; it does not show the bands forming progressively step-by-step through the loading history, so it cannot time-resolve which strain increments or which individual serrations on the flow curve correspond to which kink-band formation events.
  • The micrograph is qualitative (band inclination and trace-kink geometry only); it carries no stress or strain value of its own, so the pairing cannot quantify how much of the 45% plastic strain or which portion of the 52-80 MPa serration amplitude is attributable to kinking specifically versus other concurrent deformation (e.g. basal slip) that may also be present in the gauge.
  • Only one specimen/orientation ([0001], RT) is represented, so the pairing establishes an association for this test condition and does not by itself generalize to other orientations or temperatures.

claims n18

acta_materia_com_o10_o14
step 1 · OM
OM of the [11-20] and [01-10] specimens: straight {10-12}/{01-12} band traces plus wavy bands whose contrast is strong on the (0001) side surface and faint on (1-100)/(-2110)
step 2 · EBSD
EBSD orientation maps: lenticular bands take one uniform colour distinct from the matrix, whereas the wavy bands shade continuously with position; in the [01-10] specimen uniformly red {10-12} twins and shade-varying purple kink bands coexist

dropped by the five-panel cap: F3f, F5e, F5f

the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/orientation, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
OM alone establishes only band morphology: straight {10-12}/{01-12}-plane band traces versus wavy bands, plus an asymmetric contrast (strong on the (0001) side surface, faint on (1-100)/(-2110)) that marks the wavy bands as optically distinct from the straight ones. EBSD alone establishes only an orientation-map signature: lenticular bands each take one uniform colour (a single discrete orientation), whereas bands with the wavy morphology instead shade continuously with position (a gradually varying orientation); in the [01-10] specimen this shows up as uniformly red {10-12} twins coexisting with purple kink bands whose colour varies. Put together, the two observations show that the same population of bands -- the wavy, contrast-asymmetric ones seen in OM -- is the population whose EBSD colour varies continuously with position, while the straight, {10-12}/{01-12}-trace bands seen in OM are the population that EBSD shows as uniform single-colour (twin-like). Neither image alone links a morphology to an orientation behaviour; OM cannot say whether a band's internal orientation is uniform or graded, and EBSD orientation maps alone (without the OM band-trace/contrast record) cannot be tied to the optically distinguished straight-vs-wavy, {10-12}/{01-12}-trace-vs-other classification. The combination is what lets the two band populations (straight/uniform vs wavy/shading) be treated as one coherent pair of distinct structures rather than two separately-described but unlinked observations.
limits
  • The pair gives only a qualitative colour/contrast contrast (uniform vs continuously shading; strong vs faint side-surface contrast), not a measured magnitude of misorientation, so it does not by itself quantify how much the orientation changes across a kink band versus a twin.
  • It is drawn from two specimen orientations only ([11-20] and [01-10]) and cannot establish that the same OM-morphology/EBSD-shading pairing holds for other loading orientations or specimens.
  • The two observations are co-registered by band type (straight/lenticular vs wavy) rather than being independent measurements of the same quantity, so the match is a correspondence in imaging signature, not a mechanistic proof of what causes the continuous shading.
  • OM contrast asymmetry (strong on (0001) side, faint on (1-100)/(-2110)) and EBSD colour behaviour are two different kinds of image contrast (optical topographic/diffraction contrast vs crystallographic-orientation colour coding); their agreement in distinguishing band types does not mean they are measuring the same physical variable.

acta_materia_com_o10_o16
step 1 · OM
OM of the [11-20] and [01-10] specimens: straight {10-12}/{01-12} band traces plus wavy bands whose contrast is strong on the (0001) side surface and faint on (1-100)/(-2110)
step 2 · TEM
Bright-field TEM of the kink bands: the marked basal-plane trace bends by a large, non-constant angle at each band boundary, and many low-angle (<15 deg) boundaries coexist
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/orientation, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
OM identifies the wavy deformation bands as a morphologically distinct population from the straight {10-12}/{01-12} band traces (based on their trace shape and the surface-contrast asymmetry, strong on (0001), faint on (1-100)/(-2110)); TEM then shows that within these same bands the basal-plane trace bends by a large but non-constant angle at each boundary, with many low-angle (<15 deg) boundaries also present. Combined, this supports treating the wavy bands as a class whose internal boundary misorientation is variable rather than fixed, distinguishing them from the straight-trace bands.
limits
  • OM alone (trace geometry plus side-surface contrast) says nothing about the internal crystallographic rotation at band boundaries, so it cannot by itself distinguish a fixed-angle boundary population from a variable-angle one
  • TEM alone examines boundaries already labelled 'kink bands,' so it establishes that non-constant, large angles and many low-angle (<15 deg) boundaries coexist there, but does not by itself tie that boundary character back to the wavy-band morphology or the (0001)-side contrast asymmetry seen in OM
  • the TEM sample is described only as 'the kink bands,' so applying it to confirm the OM-identified wavy bands presupposes rather than independently tests that these are the same population
  • OM was performed only on [11-20] and [01-10] specimens, so the band-trace/contrast pattern cannot be generalized beyond those two orientations
  • the TEM description gives no count or distribution for 'many' low-angle boundaries or a numeric value for the 'large' boundary angle, so no quantitative relationship between boundary count and angle magnitude is supported by these two nodes alone

acta_materia_com_o14_o16
step 1 · EBSD
EBSD orientation maps: lenticular bands take one uniform colour distinct from the matrix, whereas the wavy bands shade continuously with position; in the [01-10] specimen uniformly red {10-12} twins and shade-varying purple kink bands coexist
step 2 · TEM
Bright-field TEM of the kink bands: the marked basal-plane trace bends by a large, non-constant angle at each band boundary, and many low-angle (<15 deg) boundaries coexist
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/orientation, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Put together, the EBSD orientation maps (lenticular bands taking one uniform colour like the {10-12} twins, versus wavy bands that shade continuously with position like the kink bands) and the TEM images (basal-plane trace bending by a large, non-constant angle at each boundary within the wavy/kink bands, with many boundaries being low-angle, <15 deg) jointly establish that the wavy bands are built from an array of boundaries whose misorientation varies continuously and non-uniformly from boundary to boundary, in contrast to the single, uniformly-oriented lenticular {10-12} twin bands that EBSD shows as one flat colour. The TEM boundary-by-boundary bending supplies the fine-scale mechanism behind the map-scale colour shading that EBSD records, while EBSD supplies the broader microstructural context (twins vs kink bands coexisting) that a single TEM image cannot provide on its own.
limits
  • EBSD colour shading alone cannot show whether the continuous orientation change arises from a discrete array of low-angle boundaries or from smooth lattice curvature without discrete boundaries; it does not measure boundary angles directly.
  • TEM alone documents bending angles and low-angle boundaries only within the specific band(s) imaged; it does not by itself show that this is the general, defining feature separating wavy bands from lenticular twin bands across the wider EBSD maps or other specimens.
  • The two observations are made on different regions/scales (EBSD full-map colour pattern vs a single TEM-imaged band's boundaries), so the pairing is not a direct co-registration of the same feature at both scales, only a convergent comparison.

claims n11

acta_materia_com_o1_o2
step 1 · SEM
SEM of the as-grown crystal: dense fine straight traces on a single alignment fill the grains, with no large precipitates
step 2 · TEM
Bright-field TEM taken with g=0002 shows strong planar fault-like contrast lying on (0001), roughly ten plates per um
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/distribution, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength descriptive
key — the combining proposition
SEM alone establishes that dense, fine, straight traces on a single alignment fill the grains with no large precipitates -- i.e., a fine aligned feature is spatially pervasive across the whole as-grown crystal, but SEM cannot identify what these traces structurally are or their crystallographic habit. TEM alone (g=0002, bright-field) establishes that the fault-like contrast lies on the (0001) plane at a local density of roughly ten plates per um, identifying the crystallographic orientation and local plate density of the feature, but this is a small-volume, local observation that on its own cannot show the feature extends through the whole crystal. Put together, the SEM traces (whole-grain, single alignment) and the TEM contrast (identified as (0001)-plane faults, ~10 plates/um) can be read as the same feature seen at two scales, supporting that the LPSO nanoplates lie parallel to (0001) and are dispersed through the whole as-grown crystal -- SEM supplies the pervasiveness/spatial extent, TEM supplies the crystallographic identity and local plate density.
limits
  • SEM gives a qualitative description of trace density and alignment across grains, with no plate count; TEM gives a quantitative local areal density (~10 plates per um) within its small field of view -- these are different kinds of quantity (whole-grain qualitative extent vs. local quantitative density) and cannot be combined into a single uniform density figure for the whole crystal.
  • The pair does not establish that the plate density is uniform throughout the crystal; it establishes only that the same aligned, (0001)-plane feature is present both broadly (SEM) and locally at ~10 plates/um (TEM), consistent with a heterogeneous (non-uniform) distribution rather than confirming homogeneity.
  • Neither image includes a scale or count that lets the SEM trace density be cross-checked numerically against the TEM plate density of ~10 plates/um; the link is qualitative (same feature, two scales), not a quantitative reconciliation.

claims n20

acta_materia_com_o2_o3
step 1 · TEM
Bright-field TEM taken with g=0002 shows strong planar fault-like contrast lying on (0001), roughly ten plates per um
step 2 · STEM:HAADF
HAADF-STEM: the plates appear as bright, heavy-atom-rich bands only a few atomic layers wide; the 1 nm inset resolves one such bright band
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
TEM (g=0002, bright-field) establishes that the basal planar defects form a dense, regularly spaced population on (0001) (roughly ten plates per um), i.e. their habit plane and population-level frequency, but diffraction/strain contrast alone cannot say whether that contrast comes from a compositional feature or from an ordinary lattice defect. HAADF-STEM establishes that an individual plate is a heavy-atom-rich band only a few atomic layers wide (Z-contrast resolved in a 1 nm inset), but on its own says nothing about how common or how widely distributed such bands are. Combined, the two observations let the planar contrast features counted in TEM be identified as heavy-atom-segregated nanoplates rather than ordinary basal stacking faults: the population seen at low magnification is the same class of object resolved compositionally at atomic scale.
limits
  • The pairing does not by itself identify which heavy elements are segregated (e.g. specific solute species) -- HAADF only shows the bands are heavy-atom-rich by Z-contrast, not their chemistry
  • The pairing does not establish the exact stacking periodicity (a specific number of atomic layers) -- HAADF only gives 'a few atomic layers wide', not a resolved layer count
  • HAADF resolves only one bright band in the 1 nm inset, so combining assumes this single resolved plate is representative of all ~10 plates per um counted in TEM, which the two images do not themselves verify
  • TEM gives a linear/areal defect density over a bulk field of view while STEM gives a local atomic-scale width/contrast measurement of one feature; matching them across scales does not itself prove uniformity of plate character across the sample

claims n8

acta_materia_com_o8_o9
step 1 · MECH:compression
Stress-strain curves: [11-20], [01-10] and [1 1 -2 1.85] all pass 5% plastic strain at RT and 300 C, [0001] fractures without yielding (x at ~355 and ~255 MPa), and only [01-10] at RT work-hardens, 165 -> 205 MPa
step 2 · OM
OM of the [1 1 -2 1.85] specimen: dense fine slip traces run parallel to the marked (0001) trace on both the (11-2 3.24) and (1-100) side surfaces
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about PRP/behavior_class, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane otherdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength conditional mechanism
key — the combining proposition
Together, the MECH data and the OM image identify a mechanism for the [1 1 -2 1.85] specimen's ductile mechanical class. MECH shows this orientation passes 5% plastic strain at both RT and 300 C without fracturing, unlike [0001] which fractures without yielding (~355 and ~255 MPa); OM on the same specimen shows dense fine slip traces running parallel to the marked (0001) trace on both the (11-2 3.24) and (1-100) side surfaces. Combined, this ties the [1 1 -2 1.85] specimen's ductile behavior specifically to basal, (0001)-plane slip activity rather than to some other unobserved process.
limits
  • Does not establish the deformation mechanism for [11-20] or [01-10], since OM is reported only for the [1 1 -2 1.85] specimen; whether those two also deform by basal slip or by a different mechanism cannot be read from this pair
  • Does not tie the slip-trace observation to a specific test temperature (RT vs 300 C) among the two conditions used in the MECH curves, since Observation B gives no temperature for the imaged specimen
  • Correlational, not causal: co-occurrence of ductility and basal slip traces on one specimen shows the traces are present, not that basal slip is the dominant or sole contributor to the measured 5% plastic strain
  • Cannot account for [01-10]'s distinct RT work-hardening (165 -> 205 MPa), since no OM is given for that orientation

attaches to the trace claim n12

acta_materia_spi_o19_o6
step 1 · MECH:compression
Basal-slip CRSS is itself raised, from ~0.5 MPa in pure Mg to ~4.3 MPa in the alloy, an ~8x increase
step 2 · MECH:compression
RT yield stress by orientation: ~9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85], ~148-165 MPa for [11-20], ~143 MPa for [01-10]; [0001] fractures at ~355 MPa without yielding
the question, as the solver sees itDoes the upstream evidence account for the downstream observation about MEC/pathway / PRP/value? Say what the combination supports and what it leaves open.
generator spine_edgedepth 2lane otherdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength conditional mechanism
key — the combining proposition
Together, the ~8x rise in basal-slip CRSS (from ~0.5 MPa in pure Mg to ~4.3 MPa in the alloy) and the strongly orientation-dependent RT yield stresses (from ~9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85] to ~148-165 MPa for [11-20] and ~143 MPa for [01-10], with [0001] fracturing at ~355 MPa without yielding) support the idea that solid-solution hardening of basal slip contributes to elevated macroscopic yield stress in orientations where basal slip is the limiting deformation mode, consistent with an alloy that is harder than pure Mg across most loading directions.
limits
  • The CRSS value is a single resolved-shear-stress number for one slip system, while the yield-stress observation spans multiple crystal orientations whose values differ by nearly 40x (~9 to ~355 MPa); the pair does not show that the 8x CRSS increase quantitatively accounts for this orientation spread, since the applied stress needed to reach a given CRSS also depends on the (unreported) Schmid factor for each orientation.
  • The very low yield stress (~9 MPa) for [1 1 -2 1.85] is not explained by the CRSS rise; a higher CRSS alone would predict higher yield stress, so orientation/Schmid-factor effects must be doing most of the work for that data point, and this is not quantified here.
  • No direct measurement links the alloy's basal CRSS to each individual orientation's yield stress; the connection is inferred, not measured pointwise.
not identifiableThe relative contribution of the raised basal CRSS versus orientation-dependent Schmid factor to the observed spread in yield stress across orientations cannot be separated from these two observations alone.

key — the combining proposition
Observation A shows that the {01-12}/{10-12} twin traces that cover the specimen after the 520 C anneal are replaced by a broad deformation band once a further 400 C anneal is applied, i.e. the anneal sequence trades twin-trace coverage for a different band morphology. Observation B shows that, in the [11-20] and [01-10] specimens, the deformation bands are optically distinguishable from twin traces: straight {10-12}/{01-12} band traces coexist with wavy bands whose contrast is strong on the (0001) side surface but faint on the (1-100)/(-2110) surfaces. Put together, the two observations support that the wavy bands seen in B are the same broad-band feature that displaces twin traces under further annealing in A, and that this band type has a morphology (wavy trace) and a surface-contrast signature (orientation-dependent, asymmetric) that sets it apart from the straight, twin-associated traces.
limits
  • The pair only documents optical trace morphology and contrast; it does not measure crystal rotation angle across the bands, so it cannot by itself show the ~5-55 deg continuously varying rotation cited as the discriminator from the ~85 deg fixed twin rotation.
  • A and B are drawn from different specimens/conditions (anneal-sequence specimen in A vs [11-20]/[01-10] loaded specimens in B); the identity of A's 'broad deformation band' with B's 'wavy band' is an inference from shared qualitative description (waviness, replacing straight twin traces), not a direct co-observation on the same specimen.
  • Neither observation examines the dislocation content of the band boundaries, so the boundary is basal-dislocation-based cannot be read off the OM trace/contrast data alone.
not identifiableWhether the wavy, orientation-contrast-asymmetric bands in B (and the broad band in A) originate from kink banding (dislocation band boundaries) or from some other band-forming process that also produces wavy, surface-dependent traces (e.g., a different twin variant or local lattice bending) cannot be separated using only the OM morphology and contrast evidence in A and B; the paper's own discriminator is the crystal rotation angle, which is not part of either observation.

key — the combining proposition
The EBSD orientation-map pattern (uniform single colour in lenticular {10-12} twin bands vs. continuously shading colour in the wavy bands, with both types coexisting in the [01-10] specimen) co-occurs with the SAED result that c-axis direction differs strongly and non-monotonically between neighbouring points across a run of wavy (kink) bands (about 60, 180, 40 and 10 deg from horizontal at points A-D). Together the two observations support treating the wavy bands as bands whose internal crystal orientation varies from point to point, in contrast to the twin bands, whose EBSD colour is uniform.
limits
  • SAED was sampled at only four points (A-D) along one run of kink bands, not densely enough by itself to distinguish a smoothly continuous rotation from a series of discrete stepped reorientations
  • SAED angles are reported relative to a fixed horizontal reference direction, not as a rotation angle relative to the surrounding matrix, so the two panels are not on a directly calibrated common scale
  • No SAED measurement is reported on the {10-12} twin bands in the same field for direct point-by-point comparison; the twin-vs-kink contrast rests on the EBSD colour uniformity alone, not on a matched SAED reading
  • EBSD colour mapping is a qualitative visualization of orientation, not itself a numeric angle, so the correspondence between 'continuous shading' and the SAED angle spread is established by spatial co-location rather than a direct overlay of the same quantity
not identifiableWhether the orientation change across the wavy bands is a smoothly continuous rotation or a series of discrete stepped reorientations cannot be separated from these two panels alone, since SAED gives only four discrete sample points
